curation.lead:
Jay Clayton is an American attorney who has occupied successive positions of extraordinary influence over the Epstein investigation, first as Chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission (2017–2020), then as Lead Independent Director and Non-Executive Chairman of Apollo Global Management (2021–2025), and currently as United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York (SDNY) appointed by President Trump in April 2025. His career trajectory maps a textbook regulatory capture arc: as a partner at Sullivan & Cromwell (1993–2017), he advised Goldman Sachs on its TARP bailout, counseled Bear Stearns on its fire sale to JPMorgan Chase during the 2008 crisis, and represented major private equity firms including Apollo. Richard Kahn, a member of Epstein's inner circle, forwarded an article about Clayton's SEC nomination to Epstein on January 19, 2017 (Finding #2951), confirming Epstein's network was tracking Clayton's appointment and its implications for the private equity industry.

Clayton's installation at SDNY in 2025 placed him atop the office investigating Epstein's financial network, despite accumulating conflicts of interest that would typically trigger recusal: he previously served as Apollo board chairman at a firm whose founder, Leon Black, paid Epstein $158 million in consulting fees; he personally represented Reid Hoffman at Sullivan & Cromwell, and Hoffman is now a named target in Attorney General Pam Bondi's directed Epstein investigation; his wife Gretchen Butler Clayton was a Goldman Sachs Vice President for 17 years; and he advised both Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan during his private practice. Attorney General Bondi specifically directed Clayton to investigate Epstein ties to Democrats including Bill Clinton, Larry Summers, Reid Hoffman, and JPMorgan—a scope that conspicuously excludes Republican-aligned figures and Clayton's own institutional relationships. Within months of his appointment, Maurene Comey, the prosecutor who led the Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell cases, was fired from SDNY (Finding #2955).

The attempt to install Clayton at SDNY is not new. In June 2020, Attorney General William Barr announced that Clayton would replace Geoffrey Berman as SDNY US Attorney while Berman was actively overseeing the Epstein prosecution, Goldman Sachs 1MDB criminal probe, JPMorgan investigation, and a Giuliani investigation (Finding #2954). Berman refused to resign; Trump fired him on June 20, 2020. Clayton withdrew from the nomination, Audrey Strauss became acting USA, and Ghislaine Maxwell was arrested twelve days later. The current installation completes what Barr attempted five years earlier, placing a lawyer with extensive ties to Epstein-linked institutions in charge of investigating those same entities.

curation.system_role: Clayton represents the perfected regulatory capture mechanism: a Wall Street lawyer who passes through the revolving door to regulatory chairmanship, rotates onto the board of an Epstein-linked firm at premium compensation immediately after governance scandal, and ultimately lands as chief prosecutor investigating the very networks he served. His career demonstrates how the private order maintains continuity across formal government transitions.

sections.title: Key Relationships
sections.content:
Clayton's position at the center of multiple networks creates what network analysts call a structural hole—bridging disconnected groups while capturing the information asymmetry between them. At Sullivan & Cromwell, he served on the Management Committee while advising the major financial institutions that would later figure in the Epstein investigation. His representation of Bear Stearns during its March 2008 fire sale to JPMorgan Chase placed his firm on the opposite side of the table from Epstein in one of the largest financial events of Epstein's life: Epstein held $55.7 million in Bear Stearns stock and lost $22.6 million in the collapse (Finding #2976). The institutional knowledge Sullivan & Cromwell gained about Bear Stearns clients during this engagement would have included awareness of Epstein as a major shareholder.

His appointment to the Apollo Global Management board in February 2021—as Lead Independent Director, then Non-Executive Chairman after Leon Black stepped down in March 2021—came during a governance overhaul following the Dechert report that exposed Black's $158 million in payments to Epstein. Board compensation totaled over $630,000 annually, including cash fees and restricted stock units (Finding #2953). Bloomberg reported that Apollo lifted board member pay at least 20 percent after the Epstein fallout. Clayton's role was explicitly framed as independent oversight; instead, it became a lucrative landing spot connecting him to the firm most directly implicated in Epstein's consulting fee arrangements.

The relationship with Donald Trump spans both social and political dimensions. LittleSis network data identifies Clayton as a golf partner of Trump (Finding #2959). Trump nominated Clayton as SEC Chairman in 2017, attempted to install him at SDNY in 2020, and finally succeeded in 2025. This relationship enabled Clayton's progression through positions of increasing influence over the Epstein investigation despite his accumulating conflicts. Clayton also maintained connections to William Barr, who orchestrated the 2020 installation attempt and whose own ties to Epstein-linked institutions—including oversight of the SDNY prosecution while Epstein died in federal custody—have been extensively documented.

sections.title: Financial Activity
sections.content:
Beyond his Apollo board compensation, Clayton's family holds significant assets through structures that raise additional conflict questions. His wife Gretchen and children hold stakes in WMB Holdings through family trusts. WMB Holdings shares an address with Corporation Service Company at 2711 Centerville Road, Suite 400, Wilmington, Delaware—the same address used by thousands of business entities, some linked to the Panama Papers (Finding #2956). Clayton's father-in-law, Daniel Butler, served as CEO of Corporation Service Company from 1975 to 1998. Public Citizen requested a Senate Banking Committee investigation in March 2017 regarding potential 18 U.S.C. § 208 conflicts of interest related to executive branch service. Estimated annual dividends exceed $4 million, with approximately $200 million in assets based on a 2 percent yield calculation.

The Bear Stearns collapse reveals the financial intersection between Clayton's institutional role and Epstein's losses. Epstein purchased 300,000 Bear Stearns shares at $97.21 on November 30, 2004, and additional shares at $106.26 on July 14, 2005, for a total purchase cost of $55,728,004.33. As the firm collapsed in March 2008, Epstein sold in tranches: 73,650 shares at $32.51 on March 14, 2008; 20,000 at $34.93; 100,000 at $32.00 on the same day; and a final 100,000 at $3.35 on March 17, 2008—the day of the JPMorgan fire sale (Finding #2976). Total sales proceeds were $33,079,369.60, producing a net loss of $22,648,634.73. While Sullivan & Cromwell advised Bear Stearns on this transaction, Epstein subsequently negotiated a BSC Stock Drop Action settlement with JPMorgan; the $3.7 million in settlement proceeds flowed through Darren Indyke's attorney trust account (Finding #2978).

Clayton's political contributions, documented in LittleSis entity 254763, reveal bipartisan cultivation: Chuck Schumer ($2,000, December 2021), Mike Crapo ($2,000, December 2021—ranking member of Senate Banking), Jim Himes ($2,000, January 2022—House Financial Services), Kevin McCarthy ($2,000, January 2022), WinRed ($5,000), French Hill ($2,000), John Kennedy ($2,000), and Thomas Kean Jr ($1,000) (Finding #2959). This donation pattern—spanning Democratic leadership, Republican leadership, and key financial services committee members—suggests strategic relationship maintenance across the political spectrum that would prove valuable during his multiple confirmation processes.

sections.title: Legal Proceedings
sections.content:
The most significant legal proceeding involving Clayton is his current role as SDNY US Attorney overseeing the Epstein investigation—a position he now occupies after two attempts at installation. The first attempt, orchestrated by Attorney General William Barr on June 19, 2020, would have placed Clayton atop the office while it was actively investigating Epstein's co-conspirators, Goldman Sachs' 1MDB criminal exposure, JPMorgan's relationship with Epstein, and Rudy Giuliani. Geoffrey Berman, then the sitting SDNY USA, refused to resign; President Trump fired him on June 20, 2020 (Finding #2954). Clayton withdrew from the nomination. The timing was significant: Audrey Strauss became acting USA, and Ghislaine Maxwell was arrested on July 2, 2020—twelve days after the failed installation attempt.

The current installation, completed in April 2025 with judicial confirmation on August 18, 2025, succeeded where the 2020 attempt failed. Attorney General Pam Bondi directed Clayton to investigate specific Epstein ties: Bill Clinton, Larry Summers, Reid Hoffman, and JPMorgan (Finding #2955). The scope conspicuously omits Republican-aligned figures and Clayton's own institutional relationships. Within this framework, Maurene Comey—the prosecutor who led the Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell cases—was fired from SDNY, reportedly leaving prosecutors "bewildered and on edge about political interference."

Clayton's conflicts of interest are structural and cumulative: (1) Apollo board chairman while Leon Black paid Epstein $158 million; (2) personal representation of Reid Hoffman at Sullivan & Cromwell while Hoffman is a named investigation target; (3) wife's 17-year career as Goldman Sachs Vice President while Goldman is a subject of investigation; (4) advisory role to JPMorgan during the Bear Stearns acquisition while JPMorgan is a named target. These conflicts would typically trigger recusal under 28 U.S.C. § 455 and DOJ conflict policies. Instead, they appear to have been positioned as qualifications for the role.

sections.title: Intelligence Activity
sections.content:
The Epstein network's awareness of Clayton's trajectory predates his SEC appointment. On January 19, 2017—the eve of Trump's inauguration—Richard Kahn, a core member of Epstein's inner circle who served as executor of Epstein's will and trustee of Gratitude America, forwarded a Seeking Alpha article to Epstein about Clayton's nomination to lead the SEC (Finding #2951). The article by Stephen Alpher noted that "attorney Jay Clayton—who has advised on numerous major P-E deals—to lead the SEC" alongside Wilbur Ross (Commerce) and Steve Schwarzman (Policy Forum chair). It also listed "Other players: OAK, APO, FIG, ARES"—APO being Apollo Global Management's ticker symbol. This corpus hit confirms Epstein's network was monitoring Clayton's appointment and its implications for the private equity industry years before Clayton would join Apollo's board.

The revolving door pattern extends beyond Clayton to the broader SEC enforcement ecosystem. Stephen Cutler, who served as SEC Enforcement Director from 2001 to 2005 before becoming JPMorgan General Counsel, managed Epstein's BSC settlement at JPMorgan while Clayton was at Sullivan & Cromwell advising Bear Stearns (Finding #1507). Both men followed the same trajectory: from SEC oversight to Wall Street, then to positions of influence over the Epstein investigation. This pattern suggests not individual corruption but institutional design—the regulatory system systematically producing outcomes where Epstein-linked personnel occupy key oversight positions.

Clayton's proximity to Epstein-adjacent intelligence operations is further suggested by Kathryn Ruemmler's surveillance of Sullivan & Cromwell personnel moves. Ruemmler, who served as Epstein's lawyer, trustee, and successor executor with over 201 documented emails to Epstein, tracked Sullivan & Cromwell partner transitions and reported them to Epstein. A December 2017 email discussed Karen Seymour's move from Sullivan & Cromwell to Goldman (Finding #1503). Clayton was on Sullivan & Cromwell's Management Committee at the same time. No direct Clayton-Ruemmler communication has been found, but the shared institutional nexus at a firm that represented multiple Epstein-linked entities creates an intelligence overlap that remains incompletely mapped.
